newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Modest turnout may hurt reformer in Russian vote.
newsitem.headline: Modest turnout may hurt reformer in Russian vote.

text.p: Modest turnout may have hurt a Russian reformer's hopes against a Communist in a vote for governor of the Nizhny Novgorod region on Sunday predicted to have a ripple effect on Russia's market reforms.
Loudspeaker trucks circled the town from early on Sunday playing rock music, and even the local head of the Orthodox Church, Bishop Nikolai, urged people to the polls.
"Indifference is one of the worst sins. I call on you to overcome this sin," he said.
On the face of it, the vote is simply to replace Boris Nemtsov, summoned by President Boris Yeltsin in March to join his team as a first deputy prime minister and speed up reforms.

But the run-off election -- a closely fought race between the reformist mayor of Nizhny Novgorod city, Ivan Sklyarov, and Communist Gennady Khodyrev -- is inevitably being seen as an unofficial referendum on Russia's painful transition to a market economy as championed by the rising star Nemtsov.
Tension was heightened by the fact that the two candidates finished almost neck and neck in the first round two weeks ago when turnout was 40 percent. Results were expected on Monday.

By 8 p.m. (1600 GMT), with polls open for another three hours, an electoral commission official said it seemed likely that the turnout would fall short of 50 percent -- the level seen by analysts as favouring Sklyarov.

"We expect that people coming from their dachas (country homes) at the end of the weekend will go to polls in the final hours, but frankly speaking I do not think 50 percent is realistic," she said, saying 42.8 percent had voted by 8 p.m.
Local journalist Mikhail Iunev added: "With this turnout the difference between the candidates may be really tiny and 10,000 votes can easily decide the winner."
Sklyarov, casually dressed, walked to vote at his polling station with his family, and approached a girl to ask her name.
"You may now shake my hand," he told the bemused youngster. "You may be shaking the hand of the future governor."
When asked whether he would continue reforms started by Nemtsov, he said: "Why just Nemtsov's reforms? There were Sklyarov reforms as well and they will certainly continue."

Nemtsov, a liberal who pioneered economic change in his region after he became governor in 1991, is now a key member of Yeltsin's reshuffled and revitalised cabinet and is widely seen as the standard bearer of radical reform and a potential successor to Yeltsin.
"If people reject reforms in his domain, how can he offer them for the rest of Russia?" the financial newspaper Birzha asked.
Nemtsov transformed Nizhny Novgorod, a city of 1.5 million people on the Volga some 420 km (260 miles) southeast of Moscow.
Clean and businesslike, the city's streets are full of new shops and crowded cafes -- a striking contrast to many other depressed and declining regional centres.
But the outcome is far from clear. The Communists still have a vast field of disciplined potential voters, many awaiting pay packets due months ago. Support is also strong in rural areas.
Communist officials from Moscow rushed to Nizhny Novgorod to back Khodyrev, 55, who ruled the region as a party chief in the late 1980s and later became a sugar trader.
Nemtsov visited the region last week to campaign for Sklyarov, who is 49 and less charismatic than his predecessor.
